explain.say: An earthquake sends out two main kinds of waves. The first, called P-waves, are fast but gentle. The strong shaking waves, called S-waves, travel more slowly behind, a bit like thunder after lightning. Which one do you think reaches you first?

faq.a: P-waves are the first earthquake waves, fast and fairly gentle, travelling at about 6 km a second in rock. S-waves come next at about 3.5 km a second and cause most of the strong shaking.
asks: Why does an earthquake warning come before the shaking?

faq.q: How does the early warning work?
faq.a: Sensors near the quake detect the fast P-waves. A computer at the Japan Meteorological Agency estimates the place and strength and sends alerts by phone, TV and radio, often seconds before the S-waves arrive.
asks: What is Japan's earthquake early warning system?
How does Japan warn people before an earthquake?

faq.q: What should you do when the alarm sounds?
faq.a: Drop to the ground, take cover under a strong desk or table, and hold on until the shaking stops. Keep away from windows. If you are near the coast after strong shaking, go to high ground in case of a tsunami.
asks: What should you do in an earthquake?

faq.q: How do bullet trains stay safe in earthquakes?
faq.a: Sensors along the lines detect the first waves and cut the power, so the trains brake automatically. A train that has slowed down is much less likely to come off the tracks.
asks: What happens to the Shinkansen in an earthquake?

faq.q: Why does Japan have so many earthquakes?
faq.a: Japan sits where four tectonic plates meet, on the Pacific Ring of Fire. About a fifth of the world’s strong earthquakes, of magnitude 6 or more, happen in or near Japan.
asks: How many plates meet under Japan?

facts: The Japan Meteorological Agency began public earthquake early warnings in 2007.
In rock near the surface, P-waves travel at roughly 6 km/s and S-waves at about 3.5 km/s.
About a fifth of the world's earthquakes of magnitude 6 or more happen in or near Japan.
